ai_context.learning_goal: Understand the basic definition and components of a quadrilateral.
common_misconceptions: Thinking any 4 connected lines make a quadrilateral.
ai_context.tutor_hint: Ask the student: 'How many diagonals can you draw in a quadrilateral?'

blocks.title: Introduction to Quadrilaterals
blocks.text: A quadrilateral is a closed figure obtained by joining four points (in order) on a plane, such that no three points are collinear. It has four sides, four angles, and four vertices.

ai_context.learning_goal: Know and use the angle sum property of quadrilaterals.
common_misconceptions: Confusing the angle sum with triangles (180°).
ai_context.tutor_hint: If they forget, ask them how many triangles fit inside a quadrilateral using one diagonal.

blocks.title: Angle Sum Property of a Quadrilateral
blocks.explanation: The sum of the four angles of a quadrilateral is always 360°. This can be proved by drawing a diagonal that splits the quadrilateral into two triangles, each with an angle sum of 180°.

ai_context.learning_goal: Apply the angle sum property to find an unknown angle.
common_misconceptions: Adding incorrectly or subtracting from 180° instead of 360°.
ai_context.tutor_hint: Prompt the user to set up an algebraic equation first before trying to subtract.

blocks.title: Finding a Missing Angle
blocks.problem: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 75°, 90°, and 75°. Find the measure of the fourth angle.
solution_steps: Let the fourth angle be x.
We know that the sum of angles of a quadrilateral is 360°.

common_misconceptions: Thinking it only needs one pair of parallel sides (that's a trapezium).
ai_context.tutor_hint: Highlight the prefix 'parallel' and ask how many pairs of opposite sides a quadrilateral has.

blocks.definition: A quadrilateral in which both pairs of opposite sides are parallel is called a parallelogram.

ai_context.learning_goal: Understand that the diagonal creates two identical, congruent triangles.
common_misconceptions: Assuming the diagonal bisects the corner angles (only true for rhombus/square).
ai_context.tutor_hint: Ask the student to trace the Z-pattern (alternate interior angles) created by the diagonal.

blocks.title: Theorem 8.1 - Diagonal of a Parallelogram
blocks.text: A diagonal of a parallelogram divides it into two congruent triangles.

ai_context.tutor_hint: Can you spot the ASA (Angle-Side-Angle) congruence criteria in the diagram?

blocks.title: Diagonal Dividing a Parallelogram
blocks.description: A visual representation showing a parallelogram ABCD with diagonal AC splitting it into triangle ABC and triangle CDA, highlighting congruent alternate interior angles.

ai_context.learning_goal: Learn the relationship between opposite sides in a parallelogram.
common_misconceptions: Forgetting that we need both pairs of opposite sides to be equal, not just one.
ai_context.tutor_hint: Remind them that Theorem 8.1 is the key to proving Theorem 8.2.

blocks.title: Theorem 8.2 and 8.3 - Opposite Sides
blocks.text:
Theorem 8.2: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal.
Theorem 8.3: If each pair of opposite sides of a quadrilateral is equal, then it is a parallelogram (Converse of 8.2).

content.tip: To prove a quadrilateral is a parallelogram, you do not always have to prove both pairs of sides are parallel. Proving that both pairs of opposite sides are equal is enough (Theorem 8.3)!

ai_context.tutor_hint: Ask: 'If I just measure the sides with a ruler and find opposite sides are equal, is it definitely a parallelogram?'

ai_context.learning_goal: Master the properties of opposite angles in a parallelogram.
common_misconceptions: Confusing opposite angles with consecutive/adjacent angles (which add up to 180°).
ai_context.tutor_hint: Ask what the sum of consecutive angles in a parallelogram is.

blocks.title: Theorem 8.4 and 8.5 - Opposite Angles
blocks.text:
Theorem 8.4: In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal.
Theorem 8.5: If in a quadrilateral, each pair of opposite angles is equal, then it is a parallelogram.

ai_context.learning_goal: Apply the opposite angles theorem to solve for algebraic variables.
common_misconceptions: Adding them and equating to 180° (treating them as consecutive).
ai_context.tutor_hint: Ask the student to draw the parallelogram to visually confirm A and C are opposite.

blocks.title: Finding Parallelogram Angles
blocks.problem: In parallelogram ABCD, if ∠A = (3x + 10)° and ∠C = (4x - 20)°, find the value of x.
solution_steps: In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal.

ai_context.learning_goal: Understand that the intersection point of diagonals cuts each diagonal exactly in half.
common_misconceptions: Thinking the diagonals are equal in length (only true for rectangles/squares).
ai_context.tutor_hint: Clarify the word 'bisect' - it means cutting into two equal parts, but doesn't mean both lines are the same length.

blocks.title: Theorem 8.6 and 8.7 - Diagonals of a Parallelogram
blocks.text:
Theorem 8.6: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
Theorem 8.7: If the diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other, then it is a parallelogram.

content.correction: A rectangle has equal diagonals. A rhombus has perpendicular diagonals. A square has BOTH equal and perpendicular diagonals. A general parallelogram has neither!

ai_context.learning_goal: Differentiate special parallelograms based on their diagonals.
ai_context.tutor_hint: Ask them to draw a very long, flat parallelogram. Are its diagonals perpendicular?

ai_context.learning_goal: Learn the most powerful shortcut to proving a quadrilateral is a parallelogram.
common_misconceptions: Thinking we need to prove both pairs are parallel, or both are equal.
ai_context.tutor_hint: Emphasize 'equal AND parallel' on the SAME pair of opposite sides.

blocks.title: Theorem 8.8 - The Single Pair Condition
blocks.text: A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if a pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel.

common_misconceptions: Applying it when points are not exactly mid-points.
ai_context.tutor_hint: Ask them what two conditions the segment must meet (parallel AND half the length).

blocks.title: Theorem 8.9 - The Mid-point Theorem
blocks.text: The line segment joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and is half of it.

ai_context.learning_goal: Calculate lengths using the Mid-point theorem.
common_misconceptions: Calculating double the length instead of half.
ai_context.tutor_hint: Ask them if DE looks shorter or longer than BC in the diagram.

blocks.title: Applying the Mid-point Theorem
blocks.problem: In ΔABC, D and E are mid-points of AB and AC respectively. If BC = 14 cm, find the length of DE.
solution_steps: Since D and E are mid-points of sides AB and AC,
By the Mid-point Theorem, DE || BC and DE = 1/2 BC.

ai_context.learning_goal: Understand the converse of the Mid-point theorem.
common_misconceptions: Confusing the theorem with its converse.
ai_context.tutor_hint: Point out the starting conditions: Theorem starts with two mid-points. Converse starts with one mid-point and a parallel line.

blocks.title: Theorem 8.10 - Converse of the Mid-point Theorem
blocks.text: The line drawn through the mid-point of one side of a triangle, parallel to another side bisects the third side.

ai_context.learning_goal: Combine the Mid-point theorem and Theorem 8.8 to solve a complex proof.
common_misconceptions: Forgetting to draw the diagonal AC to create triangles.
ai_context.tutor_hint: We know the Mid-point theorem applies to triangles. How can we turn this quadrilateral into triangles?

blocks.title: Mid-points of a Quadrilateral
blocks.problem: Show that the quadrilateral formed by joining the mid-points of the consecutive sides of a quadrilateral is a parallelogram.
solution_steps: Let ABCD be a quadrilateral and P, Q, R, S be the mid-points of sides AB, BC, CD, DA respectively.
In ΔABC, P and Q are mid-points of AB and BC. By Mid-point theorem, PQ || AC and PQ = 1/2 AC.
In ΔADC, S and R are mid-points of AD and DC. By Mid-point theorem, SR || AC and SR = 1/2 AC.
Therefore, PQ || SR and PQ = SR.
Since one pair of opposite sides (PQ and SR) is equal and parallel, PQRS is a parallelogram (Theorem 8.8).

ai_context.tutor_hint: Ask the student to recite the 5 sufficient conditions for a quadrilateral to be a parallelogram.

blocks.title: Chapter Summary
points: Sum of angles of a quadrilateral is 360°.
A diagonal of a parallelogram divides it into two congruent triangles.
In a parallelogram: opposite sides are equal, opposite angles are equal, and diagonals bisect each other.
A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if one pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel.
Mid-point Theorem: Segment joining mid-points of two sides of a triangle is parallel to third side and half of it.
